thesis.title: An Investigation of Side-Channel Security in Open-Source RISC-V Processors
thesis.institution: Birla Institute of Technology and Science (BITS) Pilani, K. K. Birla Goa Campus, Department of Computer Science and Information Systems
thesis.status: Thesis submitted (2026); degree award expected December 2026
thesis.glance: Finds new side channels in open RISC-V cores, builds a fast emulator to test defenses, and designs a verified memory encryption engine.
thesis.problem: RISC-V is open, extensible and being adopted at national scale, including India's SHAKTI and VEGA programmes. It ships without the standardized security hardening that decades of commercial pressure added to x86 and ARM, and many security-relevant behaviors (PMP, LR/SC atomics, WARL registers, performance counters) are implementation-defined. The side-channel posture of real open-source RISC-V cores was therefore largely unknown.
thesis.why: Three gaps motivated the work. No study had systematically characterized RISC-V-specific side channels across many real cores and confirmed them on silicon. No tool could evaluate microarchitectural defenses at cycle-level fidelity and still boot Linux and run large sweeps in reasonable time. And no open RISC-V memory encryption design combined confidentiality, integrity and gate-level, formally verified higher-order masking at a deployable cost.
thesis.approach: The thesis follows a discovery, evaluation and defense arc built on open, reproducible artifacts: published open cores, the Chipyard flow, cycle-model emulation and commodity Xilinx FPGA silicon. Discovery measures 23 side-channel classes on a six-core corpus with TVLA and confidence-bounded proofs of concept, then carries them to an FPGA. Evaluation builds ARCHER, an emulator calibrated against Chipyard RTL, to reproduce known attacks and compare defenses quickly. Defense designs PACE, a memory encryption engine whose masked core is proven secure by three formal tools and realized on FPGA.
thesis.thesisStatement: The openness of the RISC-V instruction-set architecture makes the security of its implementations against side-channel attacks a problem that can, and therefore must, be addressed empirically and end-to-end: the architecture's distinctive features give rise to novel side channels that can be discovered and measured on real cores; those channels and their defences can be evaluated at cycle-model fidelity with open tooling; and the resulting defensive knowledge can be realised as formally verified, low-overhead hardware, closing the loop from discovery, through evaluation, to defence.
researchQuestions: RQ1 (Discovery): Which side channels are specific to open-source RISC-V cores, how prevalent are they from in-order to wide out-of-order designs, and do they survive the move from simulation to silicon?

RQ2 (Evaluation): Can one emulation environment model microarchitectural timing faithfully enough to reproduce known attacks and evaluate defenses, yet run fast enough for large sweeps and full OS boots?

RQ3 (Defense): Can an in-line memory encryption engine for RISC-V provide confidentiality, integrity and formally verified nth-order power-analysis resistance at low overhead, validated on FPGA silicon?

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.summary: Opens with how Meltdown and Spectre in 2018 moved trust below the software line, then explains why RISC-V's openness is both a strength and a new attack surface. It reviews microarchitectural and power side channels and why main memory sits outside the trust boundary. It states three gaps, three research questions and the thesis statement, and fixes the scope to hardware side channels on open cores.
results: Three research questions organized as discovery, evaluation and defense.
Scope: microarchitectural timing and power leakage on open RISC-V; invasive and fault attacks excluded.

chapters.title: Literature Review
chapters.summary: Surveys cache and speculative-execution attacks, power and electromagnetic side channels, memory encryption and integrity, trusted execution, cryptographic ISAs, secure boot and fault injection. It then narrows to the RISC-V security literature. The synthesis argues the field is mature on closed x86 and ARM silicon but thin and largely unvalidated on real open RISC-V hardware.
results: Identifies Gap 1: no silicon-validated study of RISC-V-specific channels.
Identifies Gap 2: no evaluation tool that is both cycle-faithful and fast.
Identifies Gap 3: no practical, formally verified memory encryption for RISC-V.

chapters.title: Novel Side-Channel Attacks on Open-Source RISC-V Cores
chapters.summary: Answers RQ1 by measuring 23 side-channel classes across Rocket, VexiiRiscv, CVA6 and three BOOM widths, plus two dual-hart SoCs. Six classes are new and come from RISC-V's own features such as PMP, WARL registers, the page-table-walker fault path and LR/SC reservations. Each channel is quantified with TVLA and Wilson confidence intervals and then confirmed on a Zedboard FPGA. Eight RTL and firmware mitigations close the channels at small measured area and power cost.
results: 23 channels: 6 novel (Tier A), 7 first cross-privilege RISC-V instances (Tier B), 10 known classes (Tier C).
PMPectre: PMP-denied loads forward speculatively on out-of-order cores, timing gap up to 126 cycles, zero faults raised.
84 unit-level silicon measurements and an 11-experiment whole-core battery; amplification 2.1x to 43x on silicon.
6 of 8 mitigations cost at most 0.8% LUT area; all 8 change dynamic power by under 2 mW.

chapters.title: ARCHER: A Cycle-Accurate RISC-V Emulator for Side-Channel and Memory-Encryption Research
chapters.summary: Answers RQ2 with ARCHER, an RV64IMAFDC emulator with pluggable in-order, out-of-order and SMT cores, coherent caches and up to 16 harts, all configured through INI files. It boots Linux 6.6 in under three minutes and is calibrated against Chipyard's fab-ready RTL. On it, ten classical attacks are reproduced and evaluated against thirteen speculation policies, seven of them new. It also hosts AMES, a bus-layer memory encryption engine that is the simulation precursor to PACE.
results: 3.7x faster than gem5 DerivO3CPU (geometric mean) on bare-metal microbenchmarks.
Mean 9.4% cycle-count deviation from Chipyard RTL at a median 88x host-throughput advantage over Verilator.
Every configured defense drives leakage to zero at under 0.3% IPC loss on a full Linux boot.
Seven new speculation-defense policies across three mechanism families.

chapters.title: PACE: A Page-Adaptive, DPA-Resistant Memory-Encryption Engine for RISC-V
chapters.summary: Answers RQ3 with PACE, a TileLink engine placed between the last-level cache and memory that picks a protection policy per physical page from page-table bits. Counter-mode keystreams are precomputed while lines are cached, so evictions only XOR. Fresh re-keying and domain-oriented masking protect the engine's key against power analysis, and the masked Ascon-p S-box is proven secure by three formal tools. The engine runs on Rocket and BOOM and is placed, routed and programmed on a Xilinx XC7Z020.
results: Writeback latency reduced 9x (90 to 10 cycles); with integrity, 320 to 10 cycles.
Masked core proven order-d secure by COCO, PROLEAD and SILVER (d = 1, 2), and by COCO through d = 3.
Application-level overhead within measurement noise of plaintext for cache-resident workloads; masking adds no cycles.
Measured trace-amplification exponents 1.92/3.70/5.40/6.97 match the predicted 2(d+1) law.

chapters.title: Conclusions and Future Work
chapters.summary: Revisits the three research questions and answers each one affirmatively with the evidence of Chapters 3 to 5. It states the limits plainly: results are cycle-model-relative, rest on open cores and FPGAs rather than custom tape-outs, and PACE's DPA evidence is formal and simulated because the on-chip campaign is sensitivity-limited. It sets out future work on a physical break-then-fix, silicon-anchored calibration of ARCHER, and new RISC-V extensions.
results: Future work: co-placed sensor array and 10^5 to 10^6 trace campaign for PACE.
Future work: extend discovery to vector, hypervisor and scalar-crypto extensions and to multi-socket coherence.
Future work: compose all eight mitigations on one core and measure combined cost.

contributions: A simulation-to-silicon characterization of 23 side-channel classes on six open RISC-V cores, six of them new primitives rooted in RISC-V-specific features.
Eight RTL and firmware mitigations with measured area, power, portability and software cost.
ARCHER, an open, INI-configurable cycle-level RISC-V emulator calibrated against Chipyard RTL, with seven new speculation-defense policies and the AMES memory encryption engine.
PACE, a page-adaptive, cache-anchored memory encryption engine with confidentiality, integrity and nth-order DPA resistance, formally verified at the netlist level and realized on FPGA.
Methodology: a three-tier novelty taxonomy, a statistical-validity treatment of TVLA with Wilson intervals, and a design checklist for RISC-V implementers.
keyResults: 23 side channels across 6 cores; 6 have no x86 or ARM analogue.
PMPectre timing gap up to 126 cycles with zero architectural faults.
6 of 8 mitigations at no more than 0.8% LUT area; all 8 under 2 mW power change.
ARCHER: Linux boot under 3 minutes, 3.7x faster than gem5, 9.4% mean deviation from Chipyard RTL.
Classical Spectre-family defenses reach zero leakage at under 0.3% IPC loss.
PACE: 9x lower writeback latency; masked core proven secure through order 3; overhead within noise for cache-resident workloads.
defenseStory: Correct silicon is not safe silicon: the ISA fixes results, but timing, caches and predictors are left to the implementer, and that gap leaks.
RISC-V is open and spreading fast, but it has no standard side-channel hardening and several of its features are implementation-defined.
Discovery: 23 channels measured on six open cores, six of them new. PMP, the RISC-V memory protection unit, can be bypassed speculatively.
The channels are real: they reproduce on FPGA silicon, often stronger than in simulation, and eight small RTL fixes close them.
Evaluation: ARCHER boots Linux in under three minutes and tests a defense in minutes instead of hours, within 9.4% of real RTL timing.
Defense: PACE encrypts memory per page and hides the cipher's latency inside the cache, cutting writeback cost 9x.
Its key engine is masked and proven secure by three independent formal tools, then built on an FPGA.
Result: the security of an open ISA can be measured, reasoned about and built, at low cost.

patents.kind: Indian patent application, Complete Specification (Form 2, Section 10, Patents Act 1970)
patents.title: Hardware data-flow integrity monitor with register-file provenance tagging for RISC-V IoT processors
patents.glance: A 4-bit origin tag on every RISC-V register, checked in hardware before the value can steer a branch or a store.
patents.problem: Many attacks on IoT devices do not hijack control flow at all. They corrupt data: an untrusted input ends up as a store address, a branch target or a key, or a spoofed sensor value is used as if it had been validated. Control-flow integrity, memory tagging and pointer authentication do not track where a value came from, and software data-flow integrity costs too much on a small core.
patents.why: The thesis showed that defences for small RISC-V cores must be cheap enough to leave on all the time. Existing hardware protects only control flow or memory safety, so there was no always-on mechanism that tracks the provenance of data at the register level and enforces how data of a given origin may be used.
patents.approach: Every architectural register gets a small companion tag that records where its value came from, for example sensor-raw, sensor-validated, constant, computed, pointer, crypto-key, control or tainted (16 classes in 4 bits). When an instruction retires, a propagation unit computes the destination tag from the source tags using a programmable rules table. Loads take their tag from an address-region map, so data read from a sensor or an untrusted buffer is tagged automatically. A policy unit checks the tag whenever a register is used in a sensitive place (branch target, store address, CSR write, crypto operand) and raises a violation if that origin is not allowed there. The monitor runs beside the pipeline, so instructions that do not violate a policy pay no extra latency.
claims: A RISC-V processor with a provenance tag file holding a multi-bit tag for each integer register.

A tag propagation unit that sets the destination tag at retirement from the instruction type, the source tags and a programmable propagation rules table (an SRAM indexed by operation class and the two source tags).
An address-tag mapping table of base, mask and tag entries that tags loaded data by its source address.
A policy enforcement unit that checks tags in security-relevant contexts and raises a violation; tag work runs in parallel with execute and decode, so non-violating instructions see no added latency.
Corresponding method and IoT system-on-chip claims.
results: 230 LUTs (0.43% of the XC7Z020), 428 flip-flops, 0 BRAM, 0 DSP for 32 tags and 4 address regions.
Fmax 139.4 MHz, above the 86 MHz Konark-V core clock, so the monitor never limits the core.
0.106 W total on-chip power, of which 4 mW is dynamic.
0 cycles of added latency on non-violating instructions and 0 cycles from taint to trap; about 29 pJ per instruction (derived).
Validated on a control-data attack pattern: a tainted load used as a store address or branch target is flagged, and a clean register is not (no false positive).
patents.measurementPlatform: Implemented in Chisel on Konark-V, the authors' own dual-hart RV32IM microcontroller (153/153 core tests pass), and placed and routed with Vivado 2020.1 on a Xilinx Zynq XC7Z020 (Zedboard). Numbers are Vivado post-route output; the patent specification describes a larger instance than the one measured.
patents.abstract: A hardware data-flow integrity monitor (DFIM) for RISC-V processors that provides register-file-level provenance tagging and policy enforcement. The DFIM comprises a Provenance Tag File (PTF) that maintains a 4-bit provenance tag for each architectural register, encoding classifications such as sensor-raw, constant, computed, pointer, crypto-key, and tainted. A Tag Propagation Unit (TPU) determines provenance tags for destination registers based on instruction type and source operand tags using a programmable Propagation Rules Table (PRT) and an Address-Tag Mapping Table (ATMT) that automatically assigns tags based on memory source addresses. A Policy Enforcement Unit (PEU) checks provenance tags against a programmable Policy Table when registers are used in security-relevant contexts including branch targets, store addresses, CSR writes, and cryptographic operations. The DFIM operates in parallel with normal pipeline execution, incurring zero additional latency for non-violating instructions, and requires less than 0.01 mm^2 silicon area. The invention enables detection and prevention of data-flow attacks, including data-oriented programming and sensor manipulation attacks, without software instrumentation overhead.

patents.kind: Indian patent application, Complete Specification (Form 2, Section 10, Patents Act 1970)
patents.title: Hardware-accelerated microarchitectural event classifier with programmable feature extraction pipeline and on-chip ensemble inference engine for real-time malware detection in RISC-V processors
patents.glance: A random-forest malware detector in the RISC-V chip that reads performance counters directly, with no software agent.
patents.problem: Hardware performance counters can tell malware from benign code, but every deployed detector reads them from software. That costs 2% to 15% of CPU time, samples only every 1 to 10 ms (so short attacks fall between samples), and runs as software that malware can disable or evade by timing camouflage instructions to the sampling points.
patents.why: My doctoral work on hardware-assisted malware detection found that the weak point of counter-based detection is the software pipeline, not the idea. Moving capture, feature extraction and classification into hardware removes the overhead, the sampling gaps and the software attack surface at once.
patents.approach: A capture unit taps the performance counters through a private port, so it does not use the normal CSR read path, and produces an event-count vector per time window. A five-stage fixed-point pipeline computes mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis and entropy for each event. A random forest of decision trees, stored in programmable on-chip SRAM, is walked in parallel by one traversal unit per tree, and a majority vote gives the verdict. A resilience monitor uses CUSUM change detection and an instruction-to-event consistency check to spot malware that tries to disguise its counter profile. A Linux kernel module loads trained models and acts on verdicts; retraining only reloads the tree tables.

A pipelined fixed-point feature engine computing mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis and entropy.
An SRAM-based tree memory with parallel tree traversal units and a majority-vote aggregator, loaded through a CSR interface (for example 64 trees of depth up to 7 traversed in 7 cycles).
An adversarial resilience monitor and a per-process context tracker that tags each event vector with a process identifier.
Method claims and a RISC-V SoC claim with a Linux kernel security module.

patents.title: Per-peripheral cryptographic session engine with hardware key rotation for RISC-V IoT system-on-chip
patents.glance: Encrypts on-chip bus traffic to each peripheral with its own key, and rotates keys in hardware without the CPU.
patents.problem: Inside a system-on-chip, data between the processor and peripherals (ADCs, sensors, crypto accelerators, secure storage) travels in plaintext. Bus probing, fault injection, an open JTAG or debug port, or a hardware Trojan can read it directly. TrustZone, PMP and SiFive Shield isolate software but do not encrypt the internal bus, and none give each peripheral its own key.
patents.why: The thesis studies how hardware leaks secrets on small RISC-V systems, including memory encryption. The internal bus was the remaining plaintext path. A lightweight, single-cycle cipher makes it possible to encrypt that path at bus speed, and doing key rotation in hardware removes it as something software can forget or be tricked into skipping.
patents.approach: A key-slot register file holds a separate 128-bit session key and transaction counter for each peripheral channel; firmware loads the keys at secure boot and software cannot read them back. Each bus transaction is encrypted with PRINCE, a low-latency 64-bit block cipher, using the channel key with the transaction counter as a tweak, so the same data never produces the same ciphertext twice. A key-rotation state machine watches each counter and, at a configured threshold, derives a new key by enciphering the old one and swaps it in atomically. Small decrypt and encrypt stubs next to each peripheral complete the channel. Compromise of one channel's key does not expose the others.
claims: A RISC-V SoC with a per-peripheral cryptographic session engine on the internal bus and a key-slot register file of per-channel keys, counters and configuration bits.
A lightweight block cipher (PRINCE) performing single-cycle encryption and decryption with the transaction counter as a tweak.
An autonomous key-rotation finite state machine that derives and commits new keys when a channel's counter crosses its threshold, without processor involvement.
Peripheral-side cryptographic stubs and bus interception logic that select the key by target peripheral.
Method claims and a secure IoT SoC claim.

Derived bus-encryption throughput 2.48 Gbit/s at about 159 pJ/bit (10.2 nJ per 64-bit block).

A lightweight PRINCE block cipher engine performs single-cycle encryption and decryption of bus transactions using per-channel keys and transaction counter tweaks. An autonomous key rotation finite state machine monitors transaction counts and derives new keys when configurable thresholds are reached, without processor involvement. Peripheral-side cryptographic stubs complete the encrypted communication channel. The invention addresses security gaps in existing architectures where internal bus traffic travels in plaintext, protecting against side-channel probing, fault injection, and debug port exploitation. The compact implementation requires less than 0.03 square millimeters and less than 200 microwatts, suitable for resource-constrained IoT applications including medical devices, smart meters, and automotive systems.

patents.title: On-chip binary decision tree inference engine integrated with RISC-V trace encoder for real-time IoT security monitoring
patents.glance: Turns the RISC-V trace encoder from a passive recorder into an on-chip detector for ROP and control-flow hijacking.
patents.problem: RISC-V trace encoders (N-Trace, E-Trace) already see every branch, return and exception, but they only record and export it for offline analysis. Attacks such as return-oriented programming, code injection and control-flow hijacking finish long before external analysis can respond. ARM PAC and Intel CET do not exist on RISC-V, and software CFI is too heavy for IoT cores.
patents.why: The execution evidence needed to catch these attacks is already on the chip, in the trace path. The gap was that nothing analysed it in place. A small decision tree is cheap enough to evaluate in hardware every cycle, which gives detection without new instrumentation.
patents.approach: A feature extractor reads trace packets and keeps running counts over a sliding window of recent instructions: branch frequency, return-address consistency, instruction mix, indirect-jump target spread and interrupt rate, each quantised to 4 bits. A pre-trained binary decision tree in a small on-chip SRAM is walked node by node over these features and gives a classification within eight clock cycles. An alert controller with a confidence accumulator (several anomalous verdicts in a row before a severe response) can log, raise a non-maskable interrupt, halt into debug, or inject an alert into the trace stream. Only machine mode can update the model.
claims: A RISC-V processor with an anomaly detection engine coupled to the trace encoder output, including a trace feature extractor.
A binary decision tree inference unit with node words (leaf flag, feature selector, threshold, child pointers, class) in on-chip SRAM, giving a classification in a bounded number of cycles.
An alert and response controller with a confidence accumulator and configurable responses (log, NMI, debug halt, trace injection).
Machine-mode-only CSR interface for secure model updates.
Method claims and an IoT SoC claim.
results: Measured instance: 16-commit sliding window and 16-node tree. 307 LUTs (0.58%), 405 flip-flops, 0 BRAM, 0 DSP.
Fmax 70.6 MHz; inspects every committed instruction. 0.110 W total, 7 mW dynamic.
ROP burst detected after 13 commits (about 184 ns) with 0 false positives in the test traces.
The anomaly clears once benign instructions push the burst out of the window, which shows the O(1) sliding-window subtract works.

patents.abstract: An Anomaly Detection Engine (ADE) integrated with a RISC-V trace encoder for real-time security monitoring in Internet-of-Things devices. The ADE comprises a Trace Feature Extractor that derives behavioral metrics including branch frequency, return address consistency, instruction mix distribution, jump target dispersion, and interrupt frequency from execution trace packets. A Binary Decision Tree Inference Unit stores a pre-trained decision tree in on-chip SRAM and traverses the tree using extracted features to produce security classifications within eight clock cycles. An Alert and Response Controller generates configurable responses including logging, non-maskable interrupts, debug halt, or trace stream injection based on classification results and a confidence accumulator that prevents false-positive alerts. Machine-mode control registers enable secure model updates for adapting to evolving threats. The invention achieves sub-microsecond detection latency with less than 0.015 mm^2 area overhead and 20-100 uW power consumption at 100 MHz, enabling practical deployment in resource-constrained IoT devices.

patents.title: RISC-V processor architecture with tiered-memory ISA extension, tier-aware translation lookaside buffer, and Thunderbolt-attached external DRAM expansion with RISC-V bridge controller for Linux-based heterogeneous memory systems
patents.glance: ISA instructions and hardware page migration that let a RISC-V machine use Thunderbolt-attached DRAM as a memory tier.
patents.problem: Workloads such as LLM inference, virtual machines and EDA often need more memory than a consumer machine has. CXL memory expansion exists only on server processors. Linux can tier memory, but page migration is done in software (unmap, copy 4 KB through the CPU, update page tables, flush TLBs), which is too slow for a high-latency external tier. No ISA has instructions that know about memory tiers.
patents.why: RISC-V's custom opcode space, reserved page-table bits and custom CSRs make it possible to put tier awareness into the ISA itself. Thunderbolt 5 offers 80 Gbps on consumer hardware but had not been used for DRAM expansion with NUMA integration.
patents.approach: Layer 1 is an ISA extension, Xmtier, with tier-aware loads and stores (LD.TIER, SD.TIER), a page-migration instruction (MIGRATE), a tier statistics instruction (TIERSTAT) and a load-wait instruction (LWAIT). The TLB gains a 2-bit tier field per entry so the load/store unit can adapt to slow memory, an asynchronous load queue lets slow-tier loads proceed without stalling the core, and a hardware engine moves pages between tiers and shoots down TLB entries when done. Layer 2 is an external Thunderbolt enclosure built around a RISC-V bridge controller with custom DDR5 instructions, a latency-hiding cache with firmware prefetch and a write-snoop invalidation protocol for coherence without CXL. Layer 3 is a Linux kernel module that registers the external DRAM as a NUMA node and handles hot-plug.
claims: A RISC-V processor with the Xmtier tiered-memory ISA extension and a tier-aware TLB holding a tier field per entry.
An asynchronous load queue for non-blocking access to high-latency tiers and a hardware page migration engine with automatic TLB shootdown.
A RISC-V SoC bridge controller for connecting external DRAM over Thunderbolt or USB4, with custom DDR5 command instructions and a latency-compensating cache.
A Linux kernel integration module for ACPI SRAT/HMAT injection, NUMA node registration, hardware-accelerated migration and hot-plug.
The Xmtier encoding itself, in the RISC-V custom-1 opcode space.

Validated hot-page promotion, correct coldest-page eviction and out-of-order completion of a fast load ahead of an outstanding slow load.

Multi-port Thunderbolt bandwidth aggregation (500) increases aggregate bandwidth by address-interleaved striping across multiple ports. The invention enables RISC-V processors to transparently utilise Thunderbolt-attached DRAM for memory-intensive workloads with ISA-level support for heterogeneous memory tiering. (Figure 1)

patents.title: Programmable instruction fusion engine with SRAM-based rules table for RISC-V IoT processors
patents.glance: Macro-op fusion whose rules live in a small SRAM table, so a shipped chip can be retuned for each workload.
patents.problem: Macro-op fusion (for example LUI+ADDI into one 32-bit constant load) saves pipeline slots and energy, but in Intel, ARM, BOOM and commercial RISC-V cores the fusible pairs are hardwired. An IoT chip runs very different code (sensor filtering, cryptography, control loops, radio protocols) over a 5 to 10 year life, and a fixed rule set helps one workload and not the others.
patents.why: I wanted the benefit of fusion on small RISC-V cores without fixing the choice of patterns at tape-out. Storing rules in SRAM, written through CSRs, makes fusion a software decision, and banking the table lets each task bring its own rules.
patents.approach: A fusion detection unit sits between the fetch buffer and the decoder. Each rule entry in an SRAM table describes a pair of instructions (opcode and function-field masks), the register dependency required between them, and the fused micro-op to emit. Match logic compares the current pair against all rules in one cycle, a priority encoder picks one if several match, and a generator emits a single internal operation. A dependency check makes sure the second instruction really consumes the first one's result, so fusion never changes program meaning. The table is banked, and one CSR write switches banks at a context switch. A fusion counter supports profiling, and a constant-time mode can disable fusion for security-sensitive code.
claims: A RISC-V processor with a fusion detection unit containing an SRAM-based rules table, parallel match logic and a fused micro-op generator.
A 48-bit rule entry format: opcode and function-field masks for both instructions, register dependency flags, fused micro-op type, latency hint, priority and enable bit.
A banked rules table switched in a single cycle by a CSR write, giving zero-overhead rule-set changes at context switches.
A register-dependency verification sub-unit and a fusion statistics counter readable through a CSR.
Method claims and an IoT SoC claim with firmware that programs the rules.
results: 64-entry rules table: 155 LUTs (0.29%), 406 flip-flops, 0 BRAM, 0 DSP; Fmax 196.6 MHz; 0.107 W total, 4 mW dynamic.
1.25x effective IPC on a 400-instruction array load-accumulate loop: 80 of 400 instructions fused (20%), 400 issue slots reduced to 320.
About 20 pJ per fusion decision (derived from dynamic power and Fmax).
Validated LUI+ADDI, AUIPC+ADDI and ADD+LD fusions in-stream; a programmed pair without the required data dependency is correctly not fused.

patents.abstract: A programmable instruction fusion mechanism for RISC-V processors comprising a Fusion Detection Unit (120) positioned between a fetch buffer (115) and a decode unit (130). The Fusion Detection Unit includes an SRAM-based rules table (122) storing fusion rule entries that specify instruction patterns and register dependency requirements for fusible instruction pairs. A parallel match logic array (124) compares consecutive instruction pairs against all rule entries simultaneously in a single clock cycle. When a match is detected, a fused micro-operation generator (126) emits a single internal operation encoding both original instructions, reducing pipeline bandwidth and energy consumption. The SRAM-based storage enables runtime modification of fusion rules through a Control-and-Status Register interface without hardware changes. A banked rules table architecture supports zero-overhead switching between workload-specific fusion rule sets during context switches, making the invention particularly suitable for Internet-of-Things processors that execute diverse workloads including sensor processing, cryptography, and communication protocols. different: Every scheme gets a precise security definition and, where appropriate, a proof or reduction, and also code: theory, practice and implementation in each chapter.
Post-quantum standards (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA, and hybrid X25519 + ML-KEM-768) are taught inside the public-key chapters, not in a separate add-on chapter.

books.glance: A bottom-up textbook from the first RV64 instruction to reading and modifying the xv6 operating system kernel.
books.why: The book grew out of a gap students run into: architecture texts teach how instructions are encoded and executed but say little about privilege levels, while operating-systems texts, including the well-known xv6 commentary, show kernel code but assume the reader already knows what a CSR is, why MRET restores the program counter, or how a page-table walk interacts with Physical Memory Protection. books.audienceDetail: Readers who can program in C and have had an introductory CS course. tools.name: xv6, line by line
tools.tagline: Every line of a real operating system, explained. Every claim checked against the running kernel.
tools.glance: An interactive commentary on all 83 files of MIT's xv6-riscv, with tours, 500 questions and 25 labs.
tools.problem: Students in an operating systems course read kernel code without seeing the machine state behind it. They lose track of which stack is active, which page table is loaded, whether interrupts are on and which locks are held. Stacks, the trap path and locking are the ideas they find hardest.
tools.why: I taught operating systems at UW-Madison and KIIT and wrote a book on RISC-V and xv6 (De Gruyter Brill, 2026). I wanted a companion where no line is left unexplained and where every statement about the kernel is checked against xv6 running on QEMU, so the text cannot drift from the code.
features: All 83 source files of xv6-riscv (commit 06aad25), 13,249 lines; every non-blank line (11,666 of 11,666) is annotated
2,457 named symbols cross-referenced across C, RISC-V assembly, linker scripts and the Makefile; 229 glossary terms
52 guided tours with 1,009 steps, from make to the shell prompt, system calls, page faults, context switches, fork, exec and the log
Each tour step shows the hart, process, privilege mode, active stack and page table, interrupt state (982 strips) and held locks, recorded from xv6 under gdb
Three long-form concept pages: stacks; mode, stack and page table; locks
500 auto-graded questions in 20 categories and nine question types, each answer linked back into the annotated source

25 extension labs (trace, copy-on-write fork, mmap, superpages, ticket spinlocks, lockdep-lite, symbolic links, an e1000 driver with UDP sockets, and more), each with a reference solution as its own git branch
A seven-phase lab format with 305 self-checks, a debugging clinic of 142 real bugs, and 435 guided reveal steps; the labs add about 13,600 lines in 190 commits
Every reference solution passes its own test and xv6's full usertests on three harts
A validator re-checks every code reference against the pinned sources on each build
tech: libclang for C, hand-written scanners for assembly, linker scripts and the Makefile

tools.name: µSystem 8086
tools.tagline: A cycle-accurate 8086/8088 computer you build chip by chip, wire by wire, in a single HTML file. Boots FreeDOS.
tools.glance: A browser trainer kit: wire period 8086 chips on a canvas, assemble code, and step it cycle by cycle.
tools.problem: Microprocessor courses teach bus cycles, address decoding, interrupts and DMA, but students rarely get to wire a real system and watch the signals. Hardware trainer kits are fixed boards with fixed chips, and a wiring mistake is hard to see.
tools.why: I wanted a tool that replaces the trainer kit: students get the parts instead of a finished board, and every wire carries a real logic level. Nothing about the board is declared; the address map is found by driving the student's own decode gates, so a wrong wiring shows up the way it would on an oscilloscope.
features: CPU core is 100.00% exact on the full SingleStepTests/8088 suite: 3,007,000 cases, every documented and undocumented instruction and every undefined flag bit
Period chips placed and wired pin by pin: 8086/8088, 8284A, 8237A DMA, 8259A, 8253, 8255, SRAM/EPROM, 74LS glue logic, Hercules video, µPD765 floppy controller, XT keyboard
The PC/XT preset runs GLaBIOS from EPROM, loads the boot sector over DMA channel 2 and boots FreeDOS 1.3
Twenty-one preset boards, from a ripple counter to the PC/XT; nine ship a guided lab
Design rule checks for shorts, bus contention, floating inputs and partial decode
Step by clock half-cycle or by instruction, rewind the whole machine, probe any wire, and read a waveform analyzer
A built-in 8086 assembler; turbo mode reaches real 8088 speed
An illustrated guide of 13 sections with 570 screenshots captured from the running tool; twenty colour themes
One static HTML file, no server and no install
tools.license: GPL-3.0-or-later (embeds GLaBIOS GPL-3, FreeDOS 1.3 boot disk GPL-2+)

tools.name: NetSim
tools.tagline: A browser-based, client-side IPv4 network simulator for learning. Build topologies, watch real protocols run packet by packet, inspect every frame.
tools.glance: Build IPv4 networks in the browser, step real protocols one packet at a time, and decode every byte.
tools.problem: The hard parts of networking are the parts a textbook cannot show: timing, the state each device keeps, and what happens when things go wrong. A diagram of the TCP handshake does not show slow start backing off after a loss, and a static capture does not let a student pause, change one setting, and run it again.
tools.why: I teach computer networks and wanted Packet Tracer style topology building and Wireshark style inspection in one tool, with a clock the student controls and protocol implementations that are readable code rather than black boxes.
features: Deterministic discrete-event engine in integer microseconds, run in a Web Worker; play, run until quiet, step one event or one packet
Byte-accurate packet codecs; a sniffer on any link, layered decode with hex highlighting, and a physical-layer view (NRZ, NRZI, Manchester)
Conditional breakpoints that stop the moment a matching packet appears
Routing with static routes, RIP, OSPF and BGP (eBGP, iBGP, route reflectors); NAT with port forwarding
TCP with Tahoe, Reno, NewReno, CUBIC and SACK, with congestion window and sequence charts
DHCP, a real DNS hierarchy with a recursive resolver, and HTTP with a request waterfall
Switches with MAC learning and 802.1Q VLANs; switch logic can be replaced by sandboxed user JavaScript
802.11-style wireless with carrier sense, backoff, RTS/CTS and the hidden-node problem
Real C socket programs compiled in the browser (clang) and run on the simulated network, including fork, pthreads, select, poll and epoll
81 guided labs in 19 modules, each checked by a test that it can be completed; 40 colour themes
tech: clang in the browser for C programs

tools.name: Compy
tools.tagline: A compiler you can watch: C89 through tokens, AST, types, IR, optimization passes and RISC-V, plus a language lab for automata and parsing.
tools.glance: A C89 to RISC-V compiler in the browser that shows every phase, plus a lab for automata and parsers.
tools.problem: In a compilers course the hard part is not any single algorithm. It is holding the whole pipeline in one's head and believing that each stage does what the lecture says. A listing of LR items in a textbook is inert.
tools.why: I wrote the whole toolchain, from the preprocessor to the register allocator to the machine simulator, for this tool, so that every intermediate result is available to draw. Students can then see the state the parser is in, with the stack and the remaining input beside it, and argue with it.
features: A live phase bar: Source, Tokens, Preprocess, Parse, Types, IR, Optimize, Codegen, Run
A complete C89 preprocessor and hand-written recursive-descent parser; struct layouts drawn with padding (ILP32)
A typed three-address IR in the style of LLVM, shown as text or as a control-flow graph
Eight switchable optimization passes (simplify-CFG, mem2reg/SSA, inlining, constant folding, strength reduction, CSE, DCE, LICM) with before/after diffs
RISC-V RV32IM+F/D back end with naive and linear-scan register allocators, a live-interval chart and a machine stepper
Three execution engines (AST interpreter, IR interpreter, RISC-V simulator) over one checked process-memory model that catches null dereference, out-of-bounds, use-after-free, double free and leaks
A reversible debugger that steps forwards and backwards on all three engines

A language lab: regex to NFA to DFA to minimal DFA, FIRST/FOLLOW, grammar transformations, nine parsers (LL(1), LR(0), SLR, LR(1), LALR(1), Earley, CYK, operator precedence, recursive descent) and a PDA
32 compiler lessons and 19 language-lab lessons
Differential testing against clang -std=c89, and a 3,669-case end-to-end browser suite

tools.name: Baysik
tools.tagline: A GW-BASIC and QBasic programming environment in a single HTML file.
tools.glance: GW-BASIC and QBasic in one browser page, with real PC screen modes, sound and a full debugger.
tools.problem: Beginners need a first language with an immediate, visible result, but running classic BASIC today means installing DOSBox and finding an old interpreter. Old interpreters also give a learner little help in seeing what a program is doing.
tools.why: I learned to program on Logo and then BASIC, and wanted something I could hand to a child, a student, or an old hand without asking anyone to install anything. I also wanted a debugger that shows every frame of a recursion and lets the learner change any value.
features: One combined language: all of QBasic 1.1 plus GW-BASIC line-numbered features and some QuickBASIC extras
Every QBasic screen mode at its real resolution and colour limits (SCREEN 0 to 13), drawn with the IBM ROM fonts
PC speaker sound through Web Audio, with the full Music Macro Language for PLAY
A debugger with breakpoints, conditional breakpoints, step into/over/out, and editing of variables in any stack frame
A GW-BASIC classic console with LIST, RUN, RENUM, AUTO and soft keys
A DOS-style disk in the browser, plus optional mounting of a real folder with read-only, ask, or write permission
527 hand-written, commented programs in 21 categories
A 57-lesson tutorial in 16 units, guided tours and a language reference with runnable examples
Compiler to bytecode plus a virtual machine, so a program can pause between any two statements
tech: Vanilla JavaScript, no framework or dependencies

tools.name: Lohgo
tools.tagline: A Logo programming studio in one HTML file: turtle graphics, a debugger that walks through recursion, 68 lessons and 504 example programs.
tools.glance: A Berkeley Logo compatible studio in the browser, with turtle graphics and a recursion-aware debugger.
tools.problem: Recursion is where many learners get stuck, and Logo is where many first meet it. Without a way to see each waiting copy of a procedure, recursion stays abstract.
tools.why: Logo was my first language. I wanted a studio I could hand to a child, to a student meeting recursion for the first time, or to someone who remembers the turtle from an Apple II, with nothing to install and a debugger that shows every active frame.
features: Follows Berkeley Logo (UCBLogo), including its error wording, so books written for it work
375 primitives, each with a reference page and a runnable example
Turtle, colour and event commands from MSWLogo/FMSLogo, and multiple turtles from LCSI Logo
A debugger with breakpoints, conditional breakpoints and stepping; the call stack shows every waiting procedure with its own inputs, and values can be edited
A classic command center (listener) with history and completion
504 commented programs in 21 categories
A course of 68 lessons in 16 units, ending with building a game
Files on a browser disk, PNG export, and phone and tablet layouts
tech: Vanilla JavaScript, no framework or dependencies

tools.name: See
tools.tagline: A C89 workbench in the browser. Compile, run and step through C, and watch the stack, the heap and every pointer at real addresses.
tools.glance: A C89 compiler and debugger in the browser that draws the stack, heap and pointers at real addresses.
tools.problem: The hardest part of learning C is not syntax. It is the picture in the head: where a variable lives, what a pointer holds, why char s[] = "hi" can be changed and char *p = "hi" cannot, and what free does to a pointer that still holds the address.
tools.why: I have taught C for many years and wanted a tool that draws that picture for every program, from real bytes rather than a diagram made for the occasion, with no install, server or account.
features: Its own C89 compiler, linker and C library, running on a simulated 32-bit machine laid out like classic Unix (code at 0x08048000, stack down from 0xc0000000, i386 calling convention)
A memory picture of every stack frame, heap block, global, string literal and function, with arrows from every pointer
Stepping backwards (F8): memory, heap, frames, input and output all return to their earlier state
Every load and store is checked; null dereference, out-of-bounds, use-after-free, double free, writes to read-only data, stack overflow and dangling pointers are stopped and explained
gcc -Wall style warnings, including printf/scanf format mismatches
Watchpoints, conditional breakpoints, a hover card with the line that last wrote a value, and a raw bytes view
100 lessons in 15 units, and more than 600 commented programs in 22 categories including a find-the-bug section
A full C89 library reference, multi-file projects with real linking, and share links that carry the whole project
Phone and tablet layouts
tech: Vanilla JavaScript, no framework or dependencies

tools.name: Strux
tools.tagline: Data structures and algorithms in C89, animated from real running code.
tools.glance: 175 data structure and algorithm topics, each a real C89 function animated line by line.
tools.problem: Students rarely struggle with the idea of a linked list or a heap. They struggle with the moment: which pointer changes first, what is lost if the order is wrong, why a deleted slot in a hash table must not look empty. A whiteboard shows only the before and the after.
tools.why: I have taught data structures for many years and wanted to show every step in between, forwards and backwards, drawn from the memory of the real program rather than from a hand-made animation.
features: 175 topics in ten groups: arrays, linked lists, stacks and queues, searching, sorting, hashing, trees, balanced trees (AVL, red-black, B, B+, splay, treap), heaps and tries, graphs
Runs on See's C89 compiler and 32-bit machine; the picture is drawn from program memory after every line
A narration sentence for each step with the actual numbers, and counters for comparisons, swaps, moves, pointer steps, mallocs and frees
Memory and Calls tabs, including the recursion tree of every call made so far
Prediction questions at key moments, and a 4 to 6 question quiz per topic
Compare mode runs two topics side by side on the same data
Courses that order topics, and a graph editor for drawing one's own graph
Projector mode, dark and light themes, and phone and tablet layouts
tech: See's C89 compiler and simulated machine
